imageInfo.caption: The two ivory leaves of the consular diptych of Manlius Boethius, carved for his consulship in 487, eleven years after the last western emperor was deposed.
imageInfo.creator: Unknown Italian ivory carver; photographed by Giovanni Dall'Orto
imageInfo.source: Museo di Santa Giulia, Brescia, via Wikimedia Commons
imageInfo.note: A genuine late-fifth-century object, not a reconstruction. The inscription names NAR MANL BOETHIVS as a man of consular and patrician rank, and the consul of 487 held office under Odoacer, the Germanic commander who had deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476 and who kept the Roman calendar of offices exactly as he found it. He is generally identified as the father of the philosopher Boethius, which rests on the name and the family rather than on any statement in the sources. The consul holds the mappa, the cloth dropped to start the games, and the moneybags below his feet are the cash distributed to the crowd at his own expense. Licensed for reuse with attribution to the photographer.

summary: The Romans of the Middle Ages were the provincial populations of the former western empire who went on living by Roman law, holding Roman offices and speaking Latin under Gothic, Frankish, Visigothic and Lombard kings.
overview: After 476 the Roman state in the west disappeared and the Romans did not. They remained a legal category, a language and a landholding class for centuries, serving the kings who had replaced their emperors.
knownFor: Kept Roman law, the Senate and the consulship running under Odoacer and Theoderic.
Supplied the senatorial ministers of Gothic Italy: Symmachus, Boethius and Cassiodorus.
Were a separate legal person in barbarian law codes, with their own courts and a lower wergild.
Split into the Gallo-, Hispano- and Italo-Roman populations that became the Romance-speaking peoples.
Lost the eastern half of their own name, which the Greeks of Constantinople kept until 1453.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: In 476 Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus and sent the western imperial regalia to Constantinople. The Senate went on meeting, the consuls went on being appointed, the tax registers went on being kept, and the men who did all of this went on calling themselves Romani.

What had ended was the western emperor, not the Romans. For the next three centuries the people of Italy, Gaul, Spain and Africa lived under kings who were Goths, Franks, Visigoths, Vandals or Lombards, and who ruled them through Roman law and Roman officials because there was no other machinery available.
Rome the city and the Western Roman Empire are separate subjects here, as are the eastern Romans, who kept the name until 1453 and whom this archive files under Byzantines.

contentSections.title: Names and Identity
paragraphs: Romanus was not a nationality but a legal status and a cultural claim, and in the successor kingdoms the law turned it into something close to an ethnic label: a man was judged as a Roman or as a Goth, and the courts needed to know which.

The compounds this article uses — Gallo-Roman, Hispano-Roman, Italo-Roman — are modern scholarly conveniences and nobody in the sixth century used them. A bishop in Clermont and a landowner near Seville both wrote Romanus of themselves, with no regional qualifier, and would not have recognised the hyphens.

Their Germanic neighbours had their own word. Speakers of Germanic languages called a Latin-speaker walh, a term that has left Welsh in Britain, Wallonia in the Low Countries, Vlach in the Balkans and Wales itself: an outsider's name for Romans that long outlived the insiders' name for themselves. The Roman world as a whole was Romania, and the shard of it that Byzantine Ravenna held against the Lombards is still called the Romagna.

The awkward part is that the eastern empire never surrendered the word. Its inhabitants called themselves Rhomaioi, and when Liutprand of Cremona arrived at Constantinople in 968 as Otto I's ambassador, the emperor Nikephoros II Phokas told the westerners to their faces that they were not Romans but Lombards. Two populations claimed one name, and this archive keeps them apart as Romans and Byzantines while insisting that both claims were sincere.

contentSections.title: Roman law for Romans, Gothic law for Goths
paragraphs: The successor kingdoms ran on the personality of law: the law that applied to you depended on who you were, not on where you stood. A Goth in Italy was judged by Gothic custom and a Roman by Roman law, in the same town on the same day.

The kings therefore had to publish Roman law for their Roman subjects. Alaric II issued the Breviary of Alaric in 506, an abridgement of the Theodosian Code for the Romans of the Visigothic kingdom, and it remained the working Roman law of southern Gaul and Spain for centuries. The Burgundians produced a Lex Romana Burgundionum for the same purpose.

Being a Roman also carried a price. Salic law valued a free Frank at two hundred solidi and a Roman landowner at one hundred: the Roman was protected, counted and worth precisely half. That single figure says more about the status of the conquered population than any chronicle does.

The division ended at different times in different places. Recceswinth's Liber Iudiciorum of 654 abolished it in Spain by making one law territorial for Goth and Roman alike, while in Italy men were still declaring in charters which law they lived by into the eleventh century.

contentSections.title: The senatorial families under Theoderic
paragraphs: Theoderic ruled Italy from 493 to 526 through an explicit division of labour: Goths were the army, Romans were the administration. The great senatorial houses of Rome staffed the praetorian prefecture, the courts and the city offices, and were paid in the currency they cared about, which was rank.

Three men show how the arrangement worked and how it failed. Quintus Aurelius Memmius Symmachus was the senior figure of the Roman aristocracy and consul in 485. His son-in-law Boethius, consul in 510, translated Aristotle, wrote on music and arithmetic, and rose to be master of the offices. Cassiodorus served as quaestor and praetorian prefect and published the Variae, a collection of the official letters he had drafted in the king's name, which remains the best surviving view of how the kingdom actually administered anything.

It ended badly. Boethius defended a senator accused of treasonable correspondence with Constantinople, was charged himself, and was executed at Pavia around 524; Symmachus followed him to the block shortly afterwards. Boethius wrote the Consolation of Philosophy in prison awaiting death, and it became one of the most widely read books of the Middle Ages. The executions poisoned the relationship between the Gothic court and the Roman elite whose cooperation the kingdom depended on.

Cassiodorus outlived the kingdom he had served. He retired to his estates at Squillace in Calabria and founded the monastery of Vivarium around the middle of the century, where he set monks to copying classical and Christian texts — turning a senatorial library into a scriptorium, which is roughly how much of Latin literature survived at all.

contentSections.title: The Senate, the consulship and the offices that outlived the empire
paragraphs: The Roman Senate continued to meet in the Curia for more than a century after the last western emperor. Its members repaired public buildings, staged games, corresponded with Constantinople and quarrelled over papal elections, and Theoderic treated its approval as worth having.

The consulship survived too, and the consular diptych that leads this article is what it looked like from the outside: a man of rank gave the games, distributed money, and had his name carved in ivory and sent to his peers. The office had no power left and enormous prestige, which is why it was worth bankrupting a family for. The last consul appointed in the west took office in 534, and the last anywhere in 541, after which Justinian let the office lapse into an imperial title.

The Senate faded rather than fell. Its last recorded collective act came in the early seventh century, and by 630 the Curia itself had been converted into the church of Sant'Adriano. The building survived because it was consecrated, which is a fair summary of how most Roman institutions made it through the period.

contentSections.title: The bishop of Rome inherits the city
paragraphs: As the lay institutions thinned, the church absorbed their functions and their personnel: families that had supplied consuls began supplying bishops, and the career that had run through the prefecture now ran through the episcopate.

Gregory the Great, pope from 590 to 604, is the clearest case: a Roman of senatorial family who had served as prefect of the city before becoming a monk, and who as pope fed Rome from the papal estates, negotiated with the Lombards over the heads of the imperial officials at Ravenna, and organised the mission that converted the English. He administered Rome because the emperor's men could not.

The older civic religion had already gone. Pope Gelasius was still writing against the Lupercalia in 494, which tells us both that the old February festival was still being kept in Rome at the end of the fifth century and that it was by then a matter for argument rather than assumption.

contentSections.title: Gallo-Romans
paragraphs: The Roman population of Gaul entered the Middle Ages with its aristocracy intact and its politics local. Sidonius Apollinaris, son-in-law of an emperor and bishop of Clermont from about 470, organised the defence of the Auvergne against the Visigoths and then discovered that the imperial government had ceded the province in a treaty. His letters are the record of a class learning that no one was coming.

Under the Franks these families did not disappear; they changed employer. Gregory of Tours, bishop from 573 to 594 and author of the Histories that are the main narrative source for Merovingian Gaul, came from exactly this Gallo-Roman senatorial stock, and his book is a Roman aristocrat's account of Frankish kings.

Fusion took roughly two centuries and ran in both directions. Roman landowners took Frankish names, Frankish nobles married Roman heiresses and endowed Roman churches, and by the eighth century the legal distinction that Salic law had drawn between Frank and Roman had stopped tracking any difference anyone could see.

contentSections.title: Hispano-Romans
paragraphs: In Spain the Roman population was overwhelmingly the majority and the Visigoths a thin ruling layer, which made the barriers between them a matter of deliberate policy. Intermarriage between Goth and Roman was prohibited until Leovigild repealed the ban in the 580s, and the two groups were divided by religion as well, the Goths being Arian and the Romans Catholic.

Both barriers came down within a generation. Reccared converted to Catholicism at the Third Council of Toledo in 589, removing the religious line, and Recceswinth's Liber Iudiciorum of 654 removed the legal one by giving the kingdom a single territorial law.

The intellectual result was a Hispano-Roman writing the Goths into Roman history. Isidore of Seville, bishop from about 600 to 636, compiled the Etymologiae, an encyclopaedia that transmitted a great deal of classical learning to the rest of the Middle Ages, and also wrote a History of the Goths that presents them as the legitimate heirs of Spain. The conquered population was now supplying the conquerors with their origin story.

contentSections.title: Italo-Romans and the Lombard century
paragraphs: Italy got the harshest version of the arrangement. The Lombards entered the peninsula in 568, took the inland cities, and left the Romans divided between Lombard territory and the strip of imperial land running from Ravenna to Rome.

Lombard rule was less accommodating than Gothic rule had been. The Edict of Rothari, issued in 643, is a code of Lombard law for Lombards and does not legislate for Romans at all, which left the Roman population inside the duchies in an ill-defined position: still living by their own law, but without a king who acknowledged it.

The split hardened into geography and is still on the map. The imperial territories governed from Ravenna were Romania, the Roman land, as opposed to Lombardia; the Exarchate of Ravenna held them from 584 until the Lombards took the city in 751, and the name survives in the Italian region of Romagna.

contentSections.title: Latin becomes Romance
paragraphs: The Romans of the west were defined by their language more than by anything else, and during this period that language quietly stopped being Latin. The change was gradual and invisible to the speakers.

The Council of Tours in 813 ordered bishops to translate their homilies into the rustica Romana lingua or into German, depending on the audience. That canon is the moment the Latin west admits in writing that the spoken language of the Roman population has become something else.

The first substantial text in that something else is the Oaths of Strasbourg of 842, in which two grandsons of Charlemagne swore alliance against a third, each in the language his brother's troops could understand. The Romance of the oath is recognisably the ancestor of French, and the Romans who spoke it were on their way to becoming the French, the Spanish, the Portuguese and the Italians.

contentSections.title: What Roman civic life actually survived
paragraphs: The survival was uneven, and the parts that lasted were the parts somebody had a reason to pay for. Written law, the church's administration, tax registers, notarial practice and the habit of documenting property in writing all continued. Monumental building, public baths, professional standing armies and the aqueducts did not.

Cities contracted rather than vanished. Rome itself fell from perhaps a million people under the emperors to a few tens of thousands living in the bend of the Tiber, with the hills inside the Aurelian Walls turned over to vineyards and pasture. The town councils of curiales that had run provincial cities were crushed between imperial tax demands and the rise of the bishop, and by the seventh century the bishop was usually the effective civic authority.

Ancient buildings survived when they were given a new job. The Pantheon became a church in 609, the mausoleum of Hadrian became a fortress, and elsewhere temples became quarries and marble went into lime kilns. Roman material culture was not so much destroyed as recycled, which is why so much of it is still standing in altered form.

contentSections.title: The Gothic War and the end of the senatorial order
paragraphs: The greatest single blow to the Romans of Italy was struck by an emperor trying to liberate them. Justinian's reconquest, fought from 535 to 554, turned the peninsula into a battlefield for nineteen years; Belisarius held Rome through a siege of more than a year in 537 and 538, and the city changed hands repeatedly afterwards, with Totila taking it in 546 and the aqueducts cut.

The senatorial class did not survive the experience. Its estates were fought over, its members were killed, deported or scattered to Constantinople, and the Roman aristocracy that had staffed Theoderic's government was simply no longer there when the fighting stopped.

Justinian's Pragmatic Sanction of 554 restored confiscated property to Roman landowners and extended his law to Italy, on paper putting the Romans back in possession of their own country. Fourteen years later the Lombards arrived, and the reconquered province had neither the wealth nor the men to hold them.

contentSections.title: Charlemagne and the argument over the name
paragraphs: On Christmas Day 800 the pope crowned Charlemagne emperor of the Romans in St Peter's, and the west formally reclaimed a title it had not held since 476. The Romans in whose name this was done were the population of Italy and the papal city, and the coronation mattered to them because it gave their bishop an emperor close enough to be useful.

Constantinople was unimpressed, since it already had an emperor of the Romans and regarded a second one as an impossibility. The dispute was settled pragmatically in 812, when Byzantine envoys at Aachen acknowledged Charlemagne as basileus — emperor — while carefully withholding the words of the Romans.

The argument never really closed, and the two sides settled into calling each other names. Westerners increasingly wrote of the emperor of the Greeks, which the eastern court regarded as a deliberate insult, and easterners denied that the Franks and Lombards of the west had any claim on the word Roman at all.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: The Romans of the west did not end; they turned into other people. The Gallo-Romans became part of the French, the Hispano-Romans part of the Spanish and Portuguese, and the Italo-Romans part of the Italians, each carrying a spoken Latin that had become a separate language and a legal tradition that outlasted every kingdom that tried to govern it.

The institutional inheritance ran through the church. The papacy took the shape of a Roman office, canon law was built by men trained on Roman legal method, and when the Digest was studied again at Bologna from the late eleventh century, western Europe recovered a body of law that had never entirely stopped being used in Italy.

The name itself went east and stayed there. For the whole medieval period the people who called themselves Romans without qualification lived in Constantinople, not Rome — which is why an archive that runs from 476 to 1453 needs two articles, and why neither of them is about the empire of Augustus.

sectionImages.caption: The Palatium mosaic at Sant'Apollinare Nuovo in Ravenna, made for Theoderic early in the sixth century, whose Gothic courtiers were later cut out and replaced with curtains.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Ravennate mosaicist; photographed by Marie Thérèse Hébert and Jean Robert Thibault
sectionImages.source: Basilica of Sant'Apollinare Nuovo, Ravenna, via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: The mosaic shows the facade of Theoderic's palace, labelled PALATIVM. Figures of the Gothic king and his court originally stood between the columns; after Justinian's reconquest they were removed and curtains substituted, and hands left behind on some of the columns are still visible where the erasure was imperfect. It is the clearest surviving image of a Roman regime editing a Gothic one out of its own capital. Licensed CC BY-SA 2.0.

sectionImages.caption: A silver half-siliqua struck for Odoacer at Ravenna about 477, the year after he deposed the last western emperor, bearing his bare head and the legend FL ODOVAC.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Ravennate die-cutter; photographed by the British Museum
sectionImages.note: The portrait is bare-headed, without diadem or any imperial regalia, and the reverse carries the king's monogram in a wreath over the mintmark RV for Ravenna. Odoacer struck most of his coin in the name of the eastern emperor Zeno and kept the Roman calendar of offices, the tax registers and the Senate exactly as he found them, which is the point this article turns on: the state changed hands, the Romans did not move. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

sectionImages.caption: The incipit of the Lex Romana Visigothorum, the Roman law the Gothic kings kept for their Roman subjects, in a manuscript copied between about 950 and 1000.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown scribe
sectionImages.source: Bibliothèque du Patrimoine, Clermont-Ferrand (MS 201, fol. 11v), via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: The book is Alaric II's Breviary of 506, an abridged Theodosian Code issued for the Romans of the Visigothic kingdom and still being copied four and a half centuries later. A law book addressed to Romani is the most concrete evidence there is that Romanus was a legal category rather than a memory: the courts had to know which law a man lived by before they could hear him. Public domain.

sectionImages.section: Roman law for Romans, Gothic law for Goths
sectionImages.caption: One codex carrying the laws of the Visigoths, the Franks and the Alemanni side by side, written at the abbey of Saint Gall between 800 and 825.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown scribes of the abbey of Saint Gall; photographed by Rainer Halama
sectionImages.source: Stiftsbibliothek St. Gallen (Cod. Sang. 729), via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: Personality of law made books like this necessary: a single library needed the law of each people whose members might appear before its courts, because the law followed the person and not the ground. The same principle is what set a free Frank's wergild at two hundred solidi and a Roman landowner's at one hundred. Public domain.

sectionImages.section: The Senate, the consulship and the offices that outlived the empire
sectionImages.caption: The interior of the Curia Julia in the Roman Forum, where the Senate went on meeting for more than a century after 476, photographed in 2006.
sectionImages.creator: Photographed by Dneale52
sectionImages.date: photographed 11 March 2006; the building rebuilt about 283
sectionImages.note: The hall is Diocletian's rebuilding of about 283, and the opus sectile floor is late antique. It survives because it was consecrated as the church of Sant'Adriano in 630, a few decades after the Senate's last recorded collective act; the church fittings were stripped out in the 1930s to expose the Roman building seen here. Public domain.

sectionImages.section: The bishop of Rome inherits the city
sectionImages.caption: Gregory the Great dictating, with the dove at his ear and his scribe peering round the curtain, in a miniature painted at Trier about 983.
sectionImages.creator: The Master of the Registrum Gregorii
sectionImages.note: Painted nearly four centuries after Gregory's death and not a likeness. The scene illustrates a story from John the Deacon's ninth-century life, in which a secretary spies on the pope and sees the Holy Spirit dictating to him; the dove became Gregory's standard attribute. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: A decorated initial from one of the oldest copies of Gregory of Tours's Histories, written in the eighth century.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Frankish scribe and illuminator
sectionImages.date: 8th century; the text written between 573 and 594
sectionImages.source: Bibliothèque nationale de France (Latin 17655, fol. 79v), via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: Latin 17655 is a Corbie manuscript and one of the two earliest witnesses to the Histories, usually dated to the eighth century — within about a hundred years of the author. Gregory was a Gallo-Roman senatorial aristocrat writing the deeds of Frankish kings, which is why the main narrative source for Merovingian Gaul is a Roman book. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: A twelfth-century manuscript of Isidore of Seville's Etymologiae, from the abbey of Étival and now at Saint-Dié-des-Vosges, photographed in 2011.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown scribe; photographed by Ji-Elle
sectionImages.source: Médiathèque Victor-Hugo, Saint-Dié-des-Vosges, via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: Isidore compiled the Etymologiae in Visigothic Spain before 636 and it became one of the most copied books of the Middle Ages, which is why a Spanish bishop's encyclopaedia is on a shelf in Lorraine five hundred years later. The same author's History of the Goths gave the conquerors of his country a Roman pedigree. Licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

sectionImages.caption: King Rothari enthroned as lawgiver above a judicial duel, in a manuscript of the Lombard laws copied about 1040.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown south Italian illuminator
sectionImages.source: Biblioteca statale del Monumento Nazionale, Abbazia di Cava de' Tirreni (MS 4), via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: The Codex Legum Langobardorum, written at Benevento about four centuries after the Edict of Rothari it copies. The duel below the king is Lombard procedure, not Roman: the Edict legislates for Lombards and says nothing about the Romans living under the same dukes, who kept their own law without a king who acknowledged it. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: The Oaths of Strasbourg of 842, the first substantial text in Romance, on folio 13r of the only manuscript of Nithard's history, copied about 1000.
sectionImages.creator: Nithard; copied by an unknown scribe
sectionImages.date: the oaths sworn in 842; this manuscript about 1000
sectionImages.source: Bibliothèque nationale de France (Latin 9768, fol. 13r), via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: The Romance passage begins Pro do amur et pro xpian poblo — for the love of God and for the Christian people — and the Old High German oath follows it in the same column. Nithard, a grandson of Charlemagne, wrote both languages down because each army had to understand the oath sworn to it. The copy is about a century and a half later than the event, so the spellings are a copyist's. Public domain.

sectionImages.section: What Roman civic life actually survived
sectionImages.caption: The coffered dome and oculus of the Pantheon, which survived because it was consecrated as a church in 609, photographed in 2011.
sectionImages.creator: Anne Dirkse
sectionImages.date: photographed 15 September 2011; the building of about 125
sectionImages.note: The emperor Phocas gave the building to Boniface IV, who dedicated it as Santa Maria ad Martyres. That is the whole mechanism of Roman survival in one structure: temples that were not given a new job were quarried for marble and burnt for lime, while a consecrated building kept its roof. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

sectionImages.section: The Gothic War and the end of the senatorial order
sectionImages.caption: Gothic troops destroying Florence at Totila's order, in a fourteenth-century miniature of Giovanni Villani's Nuova Cronica.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Florentine illuminator
sectionImages.source: Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana (MS Chigi L VIII 296, fol. 36r), via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: The sack shown here did not happen: Totila besieged Florence in 542 and failed to take it, and Villani's account confuses him with Attila. The image is evidence for how the Gothic War was remembered in Italy eight centuries later, and the real damage is in Procopius — nineteen years of campaigning, Rome besieged and changing hands repeatedly, and the aqueducts cut in 537. Public domain.

sectionImages.section: Charlemagne and the argument over the name
sectionImages.caption: The stone throne in the upper gallery of the Palatine Chapel at Aachen, built for Charlemagne about 800 and photographed in 2011.
sectionImages.creator: Photographed by mibuchat
sectionImages.note: Four plain marble slabs on a stepped base, the marble reputedly brought from Jerusalem. It was at Aachen in 812 that Byzantine envoys acknowledged Charlemagne as basileus while withholding the words of the Romans, and some thirty German kings were later crowned on this seat. Licensed CC BY-SA 2.0.

sectionImages.caption: An opening of the Codex Florentinus, the sixth-century manuscript of Justinian's Digest from which the medieval revival of Roman law descends.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown scribes, probably at Constantinople
sectionImages.source: Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Florence, via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: Written within a generation of the Digest's promulgation in 533 and the oldest surviving copy of it. The book was at Pisa by the eleventh century, when the masters of Bologna began teaching from the Digest again, and was carried to Florence in 1406; the red rubrics name the jurists — Ulpian, Paulus — whose opinions the compilers excerpted. Public domain.
